items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Understanding the stability and activity of catalyst materials, such as metal oxide nanocrystals, for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is pivotal to ensuring the wide scale implementation of electrochemistry for the production of hydrogen and other important chemical feedstocks. Currently, the state-of-the-art catalysts for the OER is iridium dioxide (IrO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ). IrO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    nanocrystals exhibit moderate activity and great stability, but the scarcity of iridium limits its wide scale use. To ensure the wide-scale implementation of electrolyzers it is necessary to understand how to increase both the activity and stability of IrO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    under relevant operating conditions. Community efforts in improving the activity of IrO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    nanomaterials have highlighted that increasing structural disorder generally results in increased catalytic activity at the cost of significantly lower operational stability, creating activity-stability tradeoffs that limit widescale implementation of electrocatalysis. In this talk, I will explore how structural disorder affects the dissolution dynamics of IrO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    nanocrystals at the nanoscale via experiments that probe nanocrystal dissolution at the single nanocrystal level with liquid phase transmission electron microscopy (LP-TEM). The presence of nanoscale structural disorder, modulated via synthesis temperature and measured via geometric phase analysis, was found to increase catalytic activity as indicated by electrochemical studies. The structural disorder also had an anisotropic effect on the stability of different crystallographic facets. Increased structural disorder destabilized the OER-inactive (111) facets, while the dissolution dynamics of the OER-active (110) facets were not significantly affected. Correlation between nanoscale and device-scale observations suggested that the instability of disordered rutile IrO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    electrocatalysts was related to the increased dissolution rates of the inactive (111) facets. The increased activity observed at the device-scale was found to be related to a disorder-induced activation of the (110) facets. These observations suggest that stabilizing the (111) facets could result in active and stable disordered IrO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    -based electrocatalysts.
                  </jats:p>
title: Connecting Nanoscale and Device-Scale Characterization to Elucidate the Effects of Structural Disorder on Activity and Stability in Rutile Iridium Oxide Nanocrystals
